deep.reconstruction:
Case IV of Euler's 'tentative' theory of fluid friction (E260): a vessel kept full (cross-section ff, height a) feeds an inclined cylindrical tube (length b, section gg, angle ζ from the vertical, so cos ζ is the sine of the slope). Water leaves through an orifice of area kk at the end C, and kk is negligible against ff (𝔣 = k^4/f^4 = 0). Throughout E260 Euler uses one friction law. The wall friction in a channel of 'width' g removes, per unit length, a head α(p+l)/g. Here p is the head, α ≈ 1/4000 is a friction coefficient, and l is an additive constant head (from the next page, αl = 0.0075 ft, so l = 30 ft).

Integrating dp/ds = (driving gravity component) − α(p+l)/g along a section gives an exponential relaxation p + l − (g·slope)/α ∝ e^{−αs/g}.
- In the vessel (slope 1, width f) the head at B is A f − (1−𝔄) l, with 𝔄 = e^{−αa/f} and A = (1−𝔄)/α.
- In the tube (slope cos ζ, width g) the head at C is A𝔅f + B g cos ζ − (1−𝔄𝔅) l, with 𝔅 = e^{−αb/g} and B = (1−𝔅)/α.

The velocity head carried in the tube is 𝔤v, where 𝔤 = k^4/g^4. Because it also enters the friction term, it produces the factor (1 − αB𝔤) on the left. This yields formula §88:
v = [A𝔅f + B g cos ζ − (1−𝔄𝔅) l] / (1 − αB𝔤).

§89 takes a large, shallow vessel. Then αa/f is small, 𝔄 ≈ 1 and Af ≈ a, giving
v = [a𝔅 + (1/α)(1−𝔅) g cos ζ − (1−𝔅) l] / [1 − (1−𝔅)𝔤].
Since k ≤ g gives 𝔤 ≤ 1, and 𝔅 < 1, the denominator is positive, so the flow tends to a steady (uniform) state. If the numerator is ≤ 0 there is no outflow: the water stays at rest.

This threshold criterion is what the next page exploits. With a → 0, flow requires g cos ζ > αl, i.e. the slope must exceed αl/g. Euler then tabulates the minimum river-bed slope as a function of depth.
errors: No algebraic errors. (1/α)(1−𝔅) is B, and αB = 1−𝔅, so §89 follows correctly from §88 with 𝔄=1, Af=a. Positivity of the denominator holds because 𝔤 ≤ 1 and 𝔅 < 1.

Physically, the underlying friction law (resistance proportional to pressure head plus a constant, independent of velocity) is wrong for water. Truesdell criticised E260's model on this ground. The page's results are internally consistent but physically unfounded.
The formula in §88 is stated without derivation on this page; it relies on the general equations from earlier sections.

ideas.what: Steady outflow head for vessel plus inclined tube under a pressure-proportional friction law with additive constant l; exponential decay of head excess along each segment
ideas.modern_name: Head-loss / friction-slope analysis of pipe flow (with a non-standard, Coulomb-type friction law)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pipe-flow resistance laws: Chézy (1770s), Darcy–Weisbach (19th c.); Euler's E260 model itself is credited to Euler
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6 (1756/57, publ. 1761); discussed in Truesdell's introduction to Opera omnia II.12/13

ideas.what: Criterion that no flow occurs unless the driving head exceeds the threshold term (numerator ≤ 0 means the water remains at rest); leads on the next page to a minimum bed slope αl/g depending on depth
ideas.modern_name: Yield-stress threshold for flow (formally analogous to the critical slope ρ g h sinθ > τ_y for a Bingham/viscoplastic layer)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Bingham (1916–1922) for yield-stress fluids; critical-slope formulas for mudflows from 20th c. rheology

ideas.what: Monotonic approach to uniform motion when the denominator is positive
ideas.modern_name: Stability of the steady state of a first-order ODE for the flow

missed.claim: Euler's constant l acts as a static yield threshold. He obtains a no-flow condition g cos ζ ≤ αl, i.e. depth × slope must exceed a constant, which is formally the criterion for incipient flow of a Bingham/viscoplastic layer on an incline (h sinθ > τ_y/ρg). The model is wrong for water, but it anticipates the structure of yield-stress rheology and critical-slope criteria for mud and debris flows.
missed.quote: At si numerator fuerit vel =0, vel quantitas negatiua, aqua plane non effluet, sed in quiete perseuerabit.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest as an early, if misapplied, threshold-friction (yield) model in hydraulics. Whether historians of rheology have linked E260 to Bingham-type laws is unsure; it is probably mentioned only implicitly in Truesdell.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine specialisation of Euler's (physically incorrect) friction model, already printed and discussed in the Opera omnia. The only mildly notable point is the yield-threshold structure, which parallels later viscoplastic criteria.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image. Exponents appear as e^{−αa/f} and e^{−αb/g}, with the minus sign and fraction printed over the e. In the image the formula reads 'A𝔅f + Bg cos.ζ − (1 − 𝔄𝔅) l' and the denominator '1 − αB𝔤', consistent with the transcription.
